headline: The 6:04 Ebb: West End Bunker Draws the Blitz While East End Rip Waits on the Turn
subhead: Current speed, not water temp, is calling the shots on both ends of the ditch this week — here's how to read the clock.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

Six-point-one knots. That's what the Canal was throwing past the Bourne Bridge on the peak of Wednesday's ebb, and it tells you everything you need to know about why the bite has been a game of minutes, not hours. We're sliding toward the next neap, and every day the exchange eases a notch — the max current window shrinks, the slack water stretches a little longer on both ends, and the fish adjust accordingly. We flagged this back on the second of the month: the bass bite here stays heavily current-driven right through this lunar cycle, and the water is proving it out. When the ditch is running hard, the rips load up with bait and predators. When it's running soft, the bite goes quiet fast, and anglers who don't watch the clock end up fishing dead water without knowing it.

The East End has been the tougher read. Off the Sandwich side — the Herring Run stretch and down toward the Coast Guard station — the rip line only really turns on in that last hour and a half of the east-running tide, when the current stacks bait against the rock and creates that visible seam anglers can read from fifty yards out. Reports out of that stretch have stripers in the mix, mostly schoolies to low-slot fish, taking swimming plugs — SP Minnows and Redfins in bone and black-back — worked with the current, not against it. A few bigger fish have come on bucktails bounced along bottom right in the seam itself, but the window is short. Miss the last ninety minutes of that east tide and you're often fishing structure with no current pushing bait through it, which on this end of the Canal usually means no fish home.

The West End has been the livelier story, and it lines up with what we called two weeks back — wherever bunker pods concentrate, expect violent topwater feeds, and that pattern's held as the high pressure has stuck around. Bluefish have been all over bait schools pushed out of Phinneys Harbor on the push toward Mashnee and the Hog Island cut, with surface blitzes breaking out hard enough to see gulls diving from a half mile off. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything that throws a long cast and skips — have been the go-to when the blitz is up top. Once the bunker get pushed down or the blitz breaks up, switching to a bucktail with a curl-tail trailer and working it through the current seam off Wings Neck has kept fish coming, though the size has skewed toward bluefish over bass on that end this week. The stripers are there, but they're tucked behind the blitz, picking off cripples rather than joining the surface show.

Worth watching closely right now is what the Buzzards Bay corridor is doing with water temps, because the west end of this Canal is basically the front door to that water. The signs point to bonito trigger temperatures being close — not confirmed yet, but climbing into the range where the first fish usually show. If that arrival happens in the next several days, the west end current seams off Mashnee and Wings Neck are exactly where it'll announce itself first, usually as a fast, silent strike on small metal that nobody sees coming until the drag starts singing. I wouldn't build a trip around it yet, but I'd have a light spinning rod rigged with a half-ounce Hogy epoxy jig sitting in the rocket launcher just in case, because that fishery moves fast once it starts.

Fluke have been a quieter, more reliable side dish on the last two hours of the west end ebb, drifting the flats and channel edges around Hog Island with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, kept slow and ticking bottom. Nothing huge — most fish have run short to just barely keeper — but it's a decent way to fill dead current time between tide stages without burning gas.

The honest read: this isn't a week where you can show up whenever and expect the current to do the work for you. The neap is squeezing the windows tighter, and the difference between a good session and a skunk has come down to being on the water in that last hour and a half before the turn, on either end. East end fishing has been the tougher grind — current-dependent, short-lived, schoolie-heavy. West end has had more consistent action thanks to the bunker, but it's bluefish carrying the weight right now more than bass.

Looking ahead, expect the exchange to keep easing through the neap, which means shorter, sharper bite windows rather than long stretches of good current. I'd plan trips tight around the peak hour of whichever tide stage lines up with dawn or dusk — low light plus max current is still the best combination this ditch offers. And keep half an eye on the west end for that first bonito push. If the Buzzards Bay temps close the gap like they're threatening to, Wings Neck and Mashnee will be the first places in this whole zone to know it.
